metadata.title: Glaucoma: diagnosis and management
metadata.version: Last updated: 26 January 2022; minor changes: March 2025
metadata.summary: This guideline addresses the detection, referral, diagnosis, treatment and reassessment of glaucoma-related conditions in people aged 18 and over. It covers chronic open angle glaucoma, suspected chronic open angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension, including decisions about treatment and follow-up to limit progression and sight loss. It also addresses the organisation of eye care services and information for patients.

target_population: adults with chronic open angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension
adults at risk of developing glaucoma

Evidence of allergy to the preservative

recognition: Clinically significant ocular surface disease with symptoms

management.actions: Offer an alternative generic PGA first, followed by a beta-blocker if that is not tolerated. If neither is tolerated, offer a non-generic PGA, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, sympathomimetic, miotic or a combination of treatments.

management.severity: COAG with intolerance to pharmacological treatment
management.actions: Consider a medicine from another therapeutic class: a beta-blocker, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor or sympathomimetic. After treatment with medicines from 2 therapeutic classes, consider 360° SLT or glaucoma surgery with pharmacological augmentation (MMC) as indicated.

prophylaxis.recommendation: MMC is used during the initial stages of trabeculectomy to prevent excessive postoperative scarring and lower the risk of surgical failure.
prophylaxis.target_population: People undergoing trabeculectomy with MMC as indicated
prophylaxis.duration: During the initial stages of trabeculectomy

infection_management.prevention: Follow the cited Department of Health and Social Care guidance on limiting transmission risk in healthcare settings when using contact tonometry or gonioscopy.

therapies_index.name: 360° SLT
approved_indications: Initial treatment for newly diagnosed OHT with IOP of 24 mmHg or more when lifetime visual impairment is a risk, excluding cases associated with pigment dispersion syndrome.
Initial treatment for newly diagnosed COAG that is not advanced, excluding cases associated with pigment dispersion syndrome.

An option for COAG when satisfactory adherence and correct eye drop technique have not achieved sufficient IOP reduction, after treatment with medicines from 2 therapeutic classes, after glaucoma surgery, or when glaucoma surgery is declined or unsuitable.
A second procedure may be considered for OHT or COAG if an initially successful procedure becomes less effective over time.
therapies_index.administration: The procedure treats 360°; a second procedure may be needed later.
key_toxicities: Transient discomfort, blurred vision, photophobia and hyperaemia.
Rare complications are possible, including corneal failure.
monitoring: Assess the effect on IOP and whether its reduction remains sufficient.
If IOP rises after an initially successful procedure, assess the risk of OHT converting to COAG or COAG progressing.

therapies_index.name: generic PGA
approved_indications: OHT with IOP of 24 mmHg or more and a lifetime risk of visual impairment when 360° SLT is declined or unsuitable, interim treatment is needed while awaiting 360° SLT, or additional IOP reduction is needed after 360° SLT.
COAG when 360° SLT is declined or unsuitable, interim treatment is needed while awaiting it, or additional IOP reduction is needed after it.
Interim treatment for previously untreated advanced COAG while awaiting glaucoma surgery.
therapies_index.administration: Eye drops; demonstrate correct instillation and observe the person's technique when first prescribed.
monitoring: Assess the IOP response after starting treatment.
For COAG with insufficient IOP reduction, ask about adherence and check eye drop instillation technique.

therapies_index.name: non-generic PGA
approved_indications: An option for OHT with IOP of 24 mmHg or more when the current treatment, an alternative generic PGA and a beta-blocker cannot be tolerated.

therapies_index.name: beta-blocker
approved_indications: OHT with IOP of 24 mmHg or more when the current treatment and an alternative generic PGA cannot be tolerated.
An option from another therapeutic class when treatment does not lower IOP sufficiently in OHT or COAG, or when a person with COAG cannot tolerate pharmacological treatment.
therapies_index.administration: Topical medicines from different therapeutic classes may be used together to control IOP.
monitoring: Assess whether IOP reduction is sufficient.

therapies_index.name: carbonic anhydrase inhibitor
approved_indications: An option for OHT with IOP of 24 mmHg or more when the current treatment, an alternative generic PGA and a beta-blocker cannot be tolerated.
An option from another therapeutic class when treatment does not lower IOP sufficiently in OHT or COAG, or when a person with COAG cannot tolerate pharmacological treatment.
therapies_index.administration: Topical medicines from different therapeutic classes may be used together to control IOP.
monitoring: Assess whether IOP reduction is sufficient.

therapies_index.name: sympathomimetic
approved_indications: An option for OHT with IOP of 24 mmHg or more when the current treatment, an alternative generic PGA and a beta-blocker cannot be tolerated.
An option from another therapeutic class when treatment does not lower IOP sufficiently in OHT or COAG, or when a person with COAG cannot tolerate pharmacological treatment.
therapies_index.administration: Topical medicines from different therapeutic classes may be used together to control IOP.
monitoring: Assess whether IOP reduction is sufficient.

therapies_index.name: miotic
approved_indications: An option for OHT with IOP of 24 mmHg or more when the current treatment, an alternative generic PGA and a beta-blocker cannot be tolerated.

therapies_index.name: Latanoprost–netarsudil
approved_indications: An option identified in NICE technology appraisal guidance for reducing IOP in adults with OHT.

An option identified in NICE technology appraisal guidance for reducing IOP in adults with primary open-angle glaucoma (COAG) when a PGA alone has not reduced IOP enough, and a subsequently tried fixed-dose combination treatment has also not reduced IOP enough or a fixed-dose combination treatment containing beta-blockers is unsuitable.

therapies_index.name: preservative-free eye drops
approved_indications: OHT with preservative allergy or clinically significant, symptomatic ocular surface disease, but only when the risk of conversion to COAG is high.
An option for COAG when pharmacological treatment is not tolerated and there is evidence of preservative allergy or clinically significant, symptomatic ocular surface disease.

therapies_index.name: pharmacological treatment
approved_indications: An option for COAG when IOP remains insufficiently reduced after glaucoma surgery.
An option for COAG, including advanced COAG, when glaucoma surgery is declined or unsuitable.
therapies_index.administration: Topical medicines from different therapeutic classes may be needed concurrently to control IOP.
monitoring: Assess whether IOP reduction is sufficient to prevent progression to sight loss.

therapies_index.name: glaucoma surgery with pharmacological augmentation (MMC)
approved_indications: Advanced COAG, with pharmacological augmentation as indicated.
An option for COAG when satisfactory adherence and correct eye drop technique have not achieved sufficient IOP reduction.
An option to consider for COAG with a risk of progression to sight loss despite medicines from 2 therapeutic classes, or after intolerance to pharmacological treatment from 2 therapeutic classes.
therapies_index.administration: Glaucoma surgery with MMC augmentation when indicated; explain surgical risks and benefits. Use of MMC in these recommendations was off label in January 2022.
monitoring: Assess IOP after surgery to determine whether further treatment is needed.

therapies_index.name: MMC
therapies_index.mechanism: An antimetabolite used to limit excessive postoperative scarring and thereby reduce the risk of trabeculectomy failure.
approved_indications: Pharmacological augmentation of glaucoma surgery when indicated.
therapies_index.administration: Used during the initial stages of trabeculectomy. Its use in the specified glaucoma surgery recommendations was off label in January 2022.

therapies_index.name: trabeculectomy
therapies_index.administration: MMC may be used during its initial stages to limit excessive postoperative scarring.

therapies_index.name: glaucoma surgery
approved_indications: Further glaucoma surgery is an option for COAG when IOP remains insufficiently reduced after an earlier glaucoma operation.
monitoring: Assess whether IOP has been reduced sufficiently after surgery.

therapies_index.name: cyclodiode laser treatment
approved_indications: An option for COAG when IOP remains insufficiently reduced after glaucoma surgery.
An option for COAG, including advanced COAG, when glaucoma surgery is declined or unsuitable.

conditions.name: ocular hypertension (OHT)
conditions.description: A condition assessed for the likelihood of future visual impairment and conversion to COAG. The guideline uses an IOP threshold of 24 mmHg for referral and for treatment decisions in people at risk of visual impairment within their lifetime.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure IOP before referral.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During case-finding for COAG and related conditions.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An IOP of 24 mmHg or more is a referral criterion; consider confirming this measurement on another occasion unless urgent or emergency referral is indicated. An IOP below 24 mmHg calls for continued regular visits to a primary eye care professional.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure IOP for diagnosis and at each subsequent assessment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At diagnostic assessment and every reassessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: IOP level contributes to assessment of future visual impairment risk.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the central visual field before referral, establish its status at diagnosis and monitor for change.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Use a full-threshold or supra-threshold assessment during case-finding and a central thresholding test at diagnosis. Repeat testing when clinically indicated; a central thresholding or supra-threshold test may be used during reassessment when a central thresholding test previously documented a normal field.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A visual field defect consistent with glaucoma is a referral criterion. If a defect was previously found, retain the same measurement strategy at subsequent assessments.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Examine the optic nerve and fundus before referral and at diagnosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Use pupil dilatation during diagnostic examination and during case-finding if needed. Repeat optic nerve head assessment when clinically indicated; dilate pupils at reassessment if the optic nerve head and surrounding area cannot be seen adequately.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Optic nerve head damage is a referral criterion. A change detected on examination calls for a new optic nerve head image as a reference for later assessments.

diagnostic_workup.test: optic nerve head image or OCT
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Document the optic nerve head and provide a baseline for comparison.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Obtain imaging during case-finding if available and an optic nerve head image at diagnosis. Repeat imaging when clinically indicated or when examination identifies a change in optic nerve head status.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess peripheral anterior chamber configuration and depth.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Use during case-finding if available and at diagnosis. Repeat when clinically indicated, including after an inconclusive examination or suspected change in anterior chamber angle status.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess peripheral anterior chamber depth.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May replace gonioscopy during case-finding if gonioscopy is unavailable or the person prefers it. Use at diagnosis if clinical circumstances preclude gonioscopy, and during reassessment when clinically indicated.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess peripheral anterior chamber configuration and depth.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: An option during case-finding if gonioscopy is unavailable or the person prefers an alternative.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Contribute to diagnosis and assessment of future visual impairment risk.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At diagnostic assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: CCT is a risk factor to consider, but knowledge of corneal thickness is not required to decide whether to treat OHT.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Examine the anterior segment during follow-up.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At each assessment, with van Herick peripheral anterior chamber depth assessment when clinically indicated.

follow_up.schedule: Re-evaluate conversion and sight-loss risk at every assessment. For treated OHT with baseline IOP of 24 mmHg or more and a normal optic nerve head and visual field at the most recent assessment: if conversion is not detected or is uncertain and IOP is uncontrolled, review management and reassess between 1 month and 4 months; if conversion is uncertain and IOP is controlled, reassess between 6 months and 12 months; if conversion is not detected and IOP is controlled, reassess between 18 months and 24 months. If conversion occurs, follow the diagnosis and reassessment recommendations for COAG. Use clinical judgement within each interval, including when assessing a newly started treatment. If low lifetime visual impairment risk and acceptable IOP lead to a decision to stop treatment, offer an IOP assessment in 1 month to 4 months and further reassessment if clinically indicated.
recommended_tests: Goldmann applanation tonometry (slit lamp mounted) at every assessment.
Anterior segment slit lamp examination at every assessment, adding van Herick peripheral anterior chamber depth assessment when clinically indicated.
Repeat visual field testing when clinically indicated, using a central thresholding or supra-threshold test if a central thresholding test previously documented a normal field.
Repeat optic nerve head assessment when clinically indicated; obtain a new image if stereoscopic slit lamp biomicroscopy detects a change.
At every assessment, review general health and, when appropriate, adherence-related factors, cognitive impairment and treatment side effects.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Uncertain conversion can reflect insufficient reliable information, including inability to participate in an assessment. People who do not need treatment after referral should return to primary eye care and continue regular visits at clinically appropriate intervals.

conditions.name: suspected COAG
conditions.description: A suspected glaucoma status monitored for optic nerve head damage, visual field defects and conversion to COAG.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure IOP before referral.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During case-finding for COAG and related conditions.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An IOP of 24 mmHg or more is a referral criterion. Consider repeating the measurement on another occasion unless urgent or emergency referral is needed.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure IOP at diagnosis and during follow-up.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At diagnostic assessment and every reassessment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate visual field defects and assess possible conversion to COAG.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Use full-threshold or supra-threshold central assessment during case-finding and a central thresholding test at diagnosis, repeating if necessary to establish severity. Repeat when clinically indicated, using a central thresholding test for suspected defects or either a central thresholding or supra-threshold test if a central thresholding test previously documented normal fields.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A defect consistent with glaucoma is a referral criterion. Consider confirming a defect on another occasion before referral unless urgent or emergency referral is needed. Once a defect is detected, use the same measurement strategy at later assessments.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the optic nerve and examine the fundus.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Use during case-finding, with dilatation if needed, and at diagnosis with pupil dilatation. Reassess the optic nerve head when clinically indicated; dilate pupils if an adequate view is unavailable.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Optic nerve head damage is a referral criterion. If a change is detected, obtain a new optic nerve head image for subsequent comparison.

diagnostic_workup.test: optic nerve head image or OCT
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Record optic nerve head status for comparison.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Use during case-finding if available, obtain a baseline optic nerve head image at diagnosis and repeat imaging when clinically indicated.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess peripheral anterior chamber configuration and depth.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Use during case-finding if available and at diagnosis. Repeat when clinically indicated, including after an inconclusive examination or suspected angle-status change.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess peripheral anterior chamber depth.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: An alternative during case-finding if gonioscopy is unavailable or not preferred; use at diagnosis if gonioscopy is precluded by clinical circumstances and during reassessment when clinically indicated.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess peripheral anterior chamber configuration and depth.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: An alternative during case-finding if gonioscopy is unavailable or the person prefers it.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Contribute to diagnostic assessment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At diagnosis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Examine the anterior segment during follow-up.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At each assessment, with van Herick peripheral anterior chamber depth assessment when clinically indicated.

follow_up.schedule: At every assessment, reconsider conversion and sight-loss risk. If conversion is not detected or is uncertain and IOP is uncontrolled, review management and reassess between 1 month and 4 months; if conversion is uncertain and IOP is controlled, reassess between 6 months and 12 months; if conversion is not detected and IOP is controlled, reassess between 12 months and 18 months. After conversion, follow the COAG diagnosis and reassessment recommendations. Select the appointment within the applicable interval using clinical judgement, including the need to evaluate a newly started treatment. If low lifetime visual impairment risk and acceptable IOP lead to stopping treatment, offer an IOP assessment in 1 month to 4 months, followed by reassessment if clinically indicated.
recommended_tests: Goldmann applanation tonometry (slit lamp mounted) and anterior segment slit lamp examination at every assessment.
van Herick peripheral anterior chamber depth assessment and repeat gonioscopy when clinically indicated.
Repeat standard automated perimetry when clinically indicated, with the strategy determined by whether a defect or normal fields were previously documented.
Repeat optic nerve head assessment when clinically indicated and obtain a new image if examination detects a change.
At every assessment, review general health and, when appropriate, adherence-related factors, cognitive impairment and treatment side effects.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Uncertain conversion includes assessments lacking sufficiently accurate information. If COAG is no longer suspected after referral, discharge to primary eye care and advise regular visits at clinically appropriate intervals.

conditions.name: chronic open angle glaucoma (COAG)
conditions.description: A glaucoma condition assessed through optic nerve head status, visual fields and IOP. Progression and the likelihood of sight loss guide treatment intensity and reassessment.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Early COAG is asymptomatic. Glaucomatous sight loss produces blind spots in the visual field that may initially go unnoticed; progression can lead to symptomatic visual impairment. Lost sight cannot be restored.

subtypes.name: advanced COAG
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The guideline gives this group a distinct initial surgical treatment approach but does not specify diagnostic criteria for advanced disease.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure IOP before referral.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During case-finding for COAG and related conditions.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An IOP of 24 mmHg or more is a referral criterion. Consider repeating a measurement at or above this threshold unless urgent or emergency referral is needed.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure IOP for diagnosis and reassessment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At diagnostic assessment and every reassessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: IOP control helps guide management alongside optic nerve head and visual field changes.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify visual field defects, establish severity at diagnosis and assess progression.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Use a full-threshold or supra-threshold central assessment before referral and a central thresholding test at diagnosis, repeating it if needed to establish severity. Repeat a central thresholding test when clinically indicated during follow-up.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A glaucoma-consistent defect is a referral criterion. Consider repeating a suspected defect before referral unless urgent or emergency referral is indicated; use the same measurement strategy at subsequent assessments when a defect has been detected.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the optic nerve and examine the fundus for diagnosis and progression.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Use during case-finding, dilating pupils if necessary, and at diagnosis with pupil dilatation. Repeat optic nerve head assessment when clinically indicated; dilate pupils at reassessment if the view is inadequate.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Optic nerve head damage is a referral criterion. Document a newly detected change with a fresh optic nerve head image for future comparisons.

diagnostic_workup.test: optic nerve head image or OCT
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Record baseline optic nerve head status and support later comparison.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Use during case-finding if available; obtain an optic nerve head image at diagnosis and repeat imaging when clinically indicated or after a change is detected on examination.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess peripheral anterior chamber configuration and depth.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Use during case-finding if available and at diagnosis; repeat when clinically indicated, such as after an inconclusive result or suspected change in anterior chamber angle status.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess peripheral anterior chamber depth.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: An alternative during case-finding if gonioscopy is unavailable or not preferred; use at diagnosis if clinical circumstances rule out gonioscopy and during reassessment when clinically indicated.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess peripheral anterior chamber configuration and depth.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: An alternative during case-finding if gonioscopy is unavailable or the person prefers it.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Contribute to diagnostic assessment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At diagnosis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Examine the anterior segment during follow-up.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At every assessment, with van Herick peripheral anterior chamber depth assessment when clinically indicated.

staging.additional_rules: The guideline distinguishes advanced from non-advanced COAG for treatment but provides no formal staging definitions.

follow_up.schedule: Assess progression risk at every visit. With no detected progression and uncontrolled IOP, review treatment and reassess between 1 month and 4 months. With uncertain or detected progression and uncontrolled IOP, review treatment and reassess between 1 month and 2 months. With controlled IOP and no detected progression, reassess between 12 months and 18 months at low clinical risk or between 6 months and 12 months at high clinical risk. With controlled IOP and uncertain or detected progression, review treatment and reassess between 2 months and 6 months. Use clinical judgement to choose a time within the relevant interval, including when evaluating newly started treatment.
recommended_tests: Goldmann applanation tonometry (slit lamp mounted) and anterior segment slit lamp examination at every assessment.
van Herick peripheral anterior chamber depth assessment and repeat gonioscopy when clinically indicated.
Repeat visual field assessment with standard automated perimetry (central thresholding test) when clinically indicated; retain the same measurement strategy after a defect has been detected.
Repeat optic nerve head assessment when clinically indicated; obtain a new image if stereoscopic slit lamp biomicroscopy detects a change.
At every assessment, ask about general health and, when appropriate, adherence-related factors, cognitive impairment and treatment side effects.
long_term_effects: Progressive visual field damage may lead to visual impairment and symptomatic sight loss that cannot be reversed.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: The guideline states that most people receiving treatment for COAG retain a good quality of life and do not become blind.

conditions.name: advanced COAG
conditions.description: Advanced COAG is addressed separately because the guideline offers glaucoma surgery as its initial treatment. It does not provide criteria defining advanced disease.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish visual field severity at diagnosis and monitor progression.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Use a central thresholding test at diagnosis, repeating it if needed to establish severity; repeat when clinically indicated during reassessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: If a visual field defect has been detected, retain the same measurement strategy for later assessments.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the optic nerve and examine the fundus.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At diagnosis with pupil dilatation; repeat optic nerve head assessment when clinically indicated.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: If examination detects a change in optic nerve head status, obtain a new image for future comparison.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure IOP.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At diagnosis and every subsequent assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: IOP control contributes to assessment of progression and treatment response.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess peripheral anterior chamber configuration and depth.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At diagnosis and again when clinically indicated.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess peripheral anterior chamber depth.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Use if clinical circumstances rule out gonioscopy; include during reassessment when clinically indicated.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Contribute to diagnostic assessment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At diagnosis.

diagnostic_workup.test: optic nerve head image or OCT
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide baseline optic nerve head documentation and support later comparison.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Obtain an optic nerve head image at diagnosis; repeat imaging when clinically indicated or after examination detects a change.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Examine the anterior segment during follow-up.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At every assessment.

staging.additional_rules: No explicit threshold or staging criteria for advanced COAG are given.

follow_up.schedule: The COAG reassessment intervals also apply: without detected progression and with uncontrolled IOP, review treatment and reassess between 1 month and 4 months; with uncertain or detected progression and uncontrolled IOP, between 1 month and 2 months; with controlled IOP and no detected progression, between 12 months and 18 months at low clinical risk or between 6 months and 12 months at high clinical risk; with controlled IOP and uncertain or detected progression, review treatment and reassess between 2 months and 6 months. Choose within the relevant interval using clinical judgement.
recommended_tests: Goldmann applanation tonometry (slit lamp mounted) and anterior segment slit lamp examination at every assessment.
Repeat gonioscopy, visual field testing and optic nerve head assessment when clinically indicated.
At every assessment, review general health and, when appropriate, adherence-related factors, cognitive impairment and treatment side effects.
long_term_effects: Progressive glaucomatous visual field damage may result in irreversible sight loss.

special_populations.population: People with physical or learning disabilities or cognitive impairment
special_populations.considerations: Physical or learning disabilities may prevent participation in standard examinations. Cognitive and physical impairments should be considered when choosing management and treatment.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Use alternative assessment methods when standard methods are not feasible. If gonioscopy cannot be performed, use the van Herick peripheral anterior chamber depth assessment.

special_populations.considerations: The recommendations for initial 360° SLT exclude cases associated with pigment dispersion syndrome. The committee reported no evidence for 360° SLT in this population and considered eye drops more suitable.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For eligible people with OHT or COAG when 360° SLT is unsuitable, offer a generic PGA.

special_populations.population: People with preservative allergy or clinically significant and symptomatic ocular surface disease
special_populations.considerations: These conditions affect the choice of eye drops.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For OHT, offer preservative-free eye drops only when the person is at high risk of conversion to COAG. For COAG with intolerance to pharmacological treatment, consider preservative-free eye drops if there is evidence of preservative allergy or clinically significant and symptomatic ocular surface disease.

special_populations.considerations: Relevant comorbidities and potential drug interactions should be checked before pharmacological treatment. The guideline identifies systemic comorbidities as a possible reason to prefer a nonsurgical option when glaucoma surgery is declined or unsuitable.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For people with COAG, including advanced COAG, who prefer not to have glaucoma surgery or for whom it is unsuitable, 360° SLT is one of the treatment options.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People with OHT who are not at risk of visual impairment during their lifetime.
decision_rules: Do not initiate treatment when lifetime visual impairment is not a risk.
Advise continued visits to a primary eye care professional at clinically appropriate intervals.

not_recommended.name: Treatment for OHT
not_recommended.reason: The person is not at risk of visual impairment within their lifetime.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People with newly diagnosed OHT, IOP of 24 mmHg or more, and a risk of visual impairment within their lifetime; cases associated with pigment dispersion syndrome are excluded.
decision_rules: Assess lifetime risk of visual impairment in light of IOP, CCT, family history and life expectancy.
Offer 360° SLT as initial treatment when the eligibility criteria are met.

Explain that 360° SLT may defer eye drops and lower, but not eliminate, the likelihood of needing them. Discuss the expected time to IOP improvement, procedure-specific adverse effects and complications and their likely duration, and the possibility of another procedure.

recommended_regimens.name: 360° SLT
recommended_regimens.summary: Initial laser treatment for eligible people with newly diagnosed OHT.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The guideline's economic analysis found first-line 360° SLT more effective and less costly than eye drops, with at least 90% probability of being the more cost-effective option. High-quality evidence found no meaningful difference between 360° SLT and eye drops in attaining target IOP, health-related quality of life, overall adverse-event risk or treatment adherence.

alternative_regimens.name: generic PGA
alternative_regimens.summary: Offer eye drops when the person declines 360° SLT, the procedure is unsuitable, interim treatment is required while awaiting it, or further IOP reduction is needed after it.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: OHT with IOP of 24 mmHg or more and lifetime risk of visual impairment; unsuitability for 360° SLT can include pigment dispersion syndrome.

response_assessment.method: Measure IOP with slit lamp mounted Goldmann applanation tonometry; reassess conversion risk and risk of sight loss.
response_assessment.interpretation: Use clinical judgement to determine when to assess the effect of a newly started treatment.

supportive_care: When eye drops are initially prescribed, demonstrate their correct installation and observe the person's technique.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The committee reported no evidence for 360° SLT in pigment dispersion syndrome and considered eye drops more suitable in those cases.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People whose initially successful 360° SLT for OHT has subsequently become less effective.
decision_rules: Consider repeating 360° SLT if its earlier successful IOP-lowering effect has diminished.
The responsible consultant ophthalmologist decides whether to undertake the second procedure, considering the rise in IOP and risk of conversion to COAG.

alternative_regimens.name: 360° SLT
alternative_regimens.summary: Consider a second procedure after the benefit of an initially successful procedure declines.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Reduced effect over time after successful initial 360° SLT.

recommendations.statement: Before referring someone for investigation and diagnosis of COAG or a related condition, offer central visual field testing with standard automated perimetry (full threshold or supra-threshold); assess the optic nerve and fundus with stereoscopic slit lamp biomicroscopy, dilating the pupil if needed, and obtain OCT or an optic nerve head image if available; measure IOP with Goldmann-type applanation tonometry; and assess peripheral anterior chamber configuration and depth by gonioscopy or, if unavailable or preferred by the person, the van Herick test or OCT.
recommendations.context: Case-finding by primary eye care professionals before referral; separate from a sight test.

recommendations.statement: Do not decide to refer on the basis of IOP measured by non-contact tonometry alone.
recommendations.context: Before referral for diagnosis.

recommendations.statement: Do not refer someone previously discharged from hospital eye services after assessment for COAG or related conditions unless a change in clinical circumstances warrants a new referral.

Before deciding on referral, consider repeating visual field assessment and IOP measurement on another occasion to confirm a visual field defect or IOP of 24 mmHg or more, unless urgent or emergency referral is clinically necessary.

After considering repeat measurements, refer for investigation and diagnosis if stereoscopic slit lamp biomicroscopy shows optic nerve head damage, a visual field defect is consistent with glaucoma, or Goldmann-type applanation tonometry shows IOP of 24 mmHg or more.
recommendations.context: Referral criteria following the consideration described in recommendation 1.1.4.

recommendations.statement: Include the results of every examination and test in the referral.
recommendations.context: Referral for COAG and related conditions.

recommendations.statement: Advise people whose IOP is below 24 mmHg to keep attending their primary eye care professional regularly.
recommendations.context: Case-finding before referral.

recommendations.statement: Those planning and providing eye care services should adopt a service model that includes Goldmann-type applanation tonometry before referral for diagnosis.
recommendations.context: Service provision for COAG and related conditions.

recommendations.statement: Those planning eye care services should consider commissioning referral filtering, such as repeat measures, enhanced case-finding or referral refinement.
recommendations.context: Service provision for COAG and related conditions.

recommendations.statement: For diagnosis, offer visual field assessment by standard automated perimetry (central thresholding test), repeating it if needed to establish initial severity; dilated stereoscopic slit lamp biomicroscopy of the optic nerve and fundus; slit lamp mounted Goldmann applanation tonometry; gonioscopy to assess peripheral anterior chamber configuration and depth; and CCT measurement.
recommendations.context: Diagnosis of COAG and related conditions.

recommendations.statement: Follow relevant professional or Department of Health and Social Care guidance to limit transmission of infectious agents during contact tonometry or gonioscopy.
recommendations.context: The guideline points to Royal College of Ophthalmologists ophthalmic services guidance and Department of Health and Social Care guidance concerning CJD and vCJD transmission.

recommendations.statement: Use the van Herick assessment of peripheral anterior chamber depth when clinical circumstances prevent gonioscopy, such as inability to participate because of a physical or learning disability.
At diagnosis, obtain an optic nerve head image, such as a stereoscopic image or OCT, to establish a baseline record.
Following referral, consider an early assessment appointment when the supplied information raises clinical concern.
When diagnosing OHT, assess the likelihood of future visual impairment, considering IOP level, CCT, family history and life expectancy.

At every clinical episode, make available to all professionals involved in care prior test and image records relevant to COAG and OHT, medical history that could influence medicine selection, current systemic and topical medicines, the glaucoma medicine record, and drug allergies and intolerances.
Use alternative assessment methods when clinical circumstances prevent standard methods, including when a person with a physical or learning disability cannot participate in an examination.
Have machines and measurement instruments calibrated regularly in accordance with their manufacturers' instructions.
Account for cognitive and physical impairments when deciding on management and treatment.
Before offering drug treatment, check for relevant comorbidities and possible drug interactions.
Do not treat OHT when the person is not at risk of visual impairment during their lifetime; advise continued regular primary eye care visits at clinically appropriate intervals.

Offer 360° SLT for newly diagnosed OHT with IOP of 24 mmHg or more when lifetime visual impairment is a risk, except in cases associated with pigment dispersion syndrome. Explain that treatment can postpone and reduce, but not eliminate, the need for eye drops; discuss the expected time to IOP improvement, procedure-specific adverse effects and complications and their likely duration, and the possibility of another 360° SLT later.
recommendations.context: Initial treatment for OHT.
recommendations.rationale: The committee found first-line 360° SLT cost effective compared with eye drops; it reported no evidence for its use in pigment dispersion syndrome.

recommendations.statement: Consider repeating 360° SLT for OHT if the benefit from an initially successful procedure has diminished over time.

When first prescribing eye drops, demonstrate proper instillation and observe the person performing it correctly.
