recommendations.statement: At every assessment, offer slit lamp mounted Goldmann applanation tonometry and an anterior segment slit lamp examination with van Herick peripheral anterior chamber depth assessment when clinically indicated.
recommendations.context: Applies to COAG, suspected COAG and OHT.

recommendations.statement: Repeat gonioscopy when clinically indicated, including after an inconclusive examination or when a change in anterior chamber angle status is suspected.

When clinically indicated, repeat visual field testing with standard automated perimetry (central thresholding test) in COAG and in people with suspected visual field defects being investigated for possible COAG.
recommendations.context: Recommended reassessment intervals are addressed in table 2 and table 3.

recommendations.statement: When clinically indicated, repeat visual field testing with either a central thresholding or a supra-threshold test for OHT or suspected COAG if standard threshold automated perimetry (central thresholding test) previously documented normal visual fields.
recommendations.context: Recommended reassessment intervals are addressed in table 1 and table 2.

recommendations.statement: After a visual field defect has been identified, retain the same measurement strategy for every subsequent visual field assessment.
Repeat optic nerve head assessment, such as stereoscopic slit lamp biomicroscopy or imaging, when clinically indicated.
If stereoscopic slit lamp biomicroscopy identifies a change in optic nerve head status, obtain another optic nerve head image for the person's records as a new comparison baseline.
If the optic nerve head and surrounding area cannot be viewed adequately at reassessment, dilate the person's pupils before repeating stereoscopic slit lamp biomicroscopy or optic nerve head imaging.
At each assessment, reconsider the risks of conversion to COAG and sight loss when determining the next assessment date.
recommendations.context: Applies to COAG, suspected COAG and OHT.

recommendations.statement: At every assessment, ask about general health and, where appropriate, factors affecting treatment adherence, including cognitive impairment and treatment adverse effects.
recommendations.context: Applies to COAG, suspected COAG and OHT.

recommendations.statement: For treated OHT with baseline IOP of 24 mmHg or more and a normal optic nerve head and visual field at the latest assessment, use clinical judgement to assess IOP control and conversion risk, then follow table 1: if conversion is not detected or is uncertain and IOP is uncontrolled, review management and reassess between 1 month and 4 months; if conversion is uncertain and IOP is controlled, reassess between 6 months and 12 months; if conversion is not detected and IOP is controlled, reassess between 18 months and 24 months; if conversion occurs, follow the COAG diagnosis and reassessment recommendations.
recommendations.context: Use clinical judgement to select an appointment within the stated interval, including to evaluate newly started treatment. Uncertain conversion includes insufficient accurate assessment information.
recommendations.source_heading: People with treated OHT (baseline IOP 24 mmHg or more) and a normal optic nerve head and visual field at most recent assessment

recommendations.statement: For suspected COAG, use clinical judgement to evaluate IOP control and conversion risk based on optic nerve head damage and visual field defect, then follow table 2: with no detected or uncertain conversion and uncontrolled IOP, review management and reassess between 1 month and 4 months; with uncertain conversion and controlled IOP, reassess between 6 months and 12 months; with no detected conversion and controlled IOP, reassess between 12 months and 18 months; if conversion occurs, follow the COAG diagnosis and reassessment recommendations.
recommendations.context: Use clinical judgement within the interval, including when assessing newly started treatment. Uncertain conversion includes insufficient accurate assessment information.

recommendations.statement: For COAG, use clinical judgement to assess progression risk and follow table 3: if progression is not detected but IOP is uncontrolled, review treatment and reassess between 1 month and 4 months; if progression is uncertain or present and IOP is uncontrolled, review treatment and reassess between 1 month and 2 months; if progression is not detected, IOP is controlled and clinical risk is low, reassess between 12 months and 18 months; if risk is high instead, reassess between 6 months and 12 months; if progression is uncertain or present despite controlled IOP, review treatment and reassess between 2 months and 6 months.
recommendations.context: Use clinical judgement within the interval, including when assessing newly started treatment.

recommendations.statement: Discharge to primary eye care services if a person referred for OHT does not require treatment or a person referred for suspected COAG is no longer suspected of having it. Advise continued regular primary eye care visits at clinically appropriate intervals.

Provide a discharge summary to anyone assessed and returned to primary care; send a copy to their GP and, with the person's consent, relevant information to their nominated primary eye care professional. Advise the person to bring the summary to future sight tests.

Refer to a consultant ophthalmologist for consideration of a definitive diagnosis and management plan when optic nerve damage or a repeatable visual field defect is suspected, or when SLT is suitable.
recommendations.context: The SLT criterion refers to newly diagnosed OHT and COAG as described in recommendations 1.4.4 and 1.4.17.
recommendations.rationale: The committee specified consultant referral when 360° SLT is suitable.

recommendations.statement: Diagnosis and management planning for OHT and suspected COAG should be undertaken by a healthcare professional with a specialist qualification and relevant experience.

Recognise that an independent or non-medical prescribing qualification on its own does not qualify a professional to manage glaucoma and related conditions without a specialist qualification appropriate to the case's complexity.

Professionals diagnosing OHT or suspected COAG, or preliminarily identifying COAG, should be trained in detection and referral refinement, recognise abnormalities from relevant clinical assessments, understand diagnostic principles, and perform and interpret medical and ocular history, differential diagnosis, slit lamp mounted Goldmann applanation tonometry, standard automated perimetry (central thresholding test), central supra-threshold perimetry, stereoscopic slit lamp biomicroscopy of the anterior segment, posterior segment examination by slit lamp binocular indirect ophthalmoscopy, gonioscopy, van Herick peripheral anterior chamber depth assessment and CCT measurement.

Monitoring and treatment of OHT, suspected COAG or COAG should be provided by a trained professional who has a specialist qualification, relevant experience and the ability to recognise changes in clinical status.

Professionals monitoring and treating OHT, suspected COAG and established COAG should be trained to decide management using conversion risk factors, coexisting pathology, risk of sight loss, monitoring and detection of clinical changes, pharmacology of IOP-lowering medicines, eligibility for 360° SLT, and treatment changes with relevant contraindications and interactions considered.
recommendations.context: Detection of clinical change includes visual field findings and stereoscopic slit lamp biomicroscopy of anterior and posterior segments.

recommendations.statement: Professionals should discuss both offering and performing 360° SLT with the responsible consultant ophthalmologist, who should support those undertaking it. Training should cover procedural suitability, laser safety and procedures, benefits and risks and their discussion with patients and, where appropriate, families or carers, and patient consent.
recommendations.rationale: The committee identified consultant support and relevant training as safeguards for delivery of 360° SLT.

recommendations.statement: Once OHT or suspected COAG is confirmed and a management plan established, a suitably trained professional may monitor, but not treat, the person if they know OHT and COAG, have relevant experience, can detect clinical change, and can perform and interpret slit lamp mounted Goldmann applanation tonometry, standard automated perimetry (central thresholding test), central supra-threshold perimetry, stereoscopic slit lamp biomicroscopy of the anterior segment, van Herick peripheral anterior chamber depth assessment and posterior segment examination by slit lamp binocular indirect ophthalmoscopy.
recommendations.context: Central supra-threshold perimetry may be used for monitoring when the visual field is normal.

recommendations.statement: Professionals who independently diagnose, treat or monitor without consultant ophthalmologist supervision should assume full responsibility for the care they deliver.

Offer people opportunities to discuss diagnosis, referral, prognosis, treatment and discharge, and provide accessible information at initial and later visits. Cover their condition and lifelong implications, prospects for retaining sight, the absence of symptoms in OHT, suspected COAG and early COAG, the good quality of life and avoidance of blindness for most people treated for COAG, the irreversibility of lost sight, treatment choices and their action, adverse effects, risks and benefits, the possibility of familial glaucoma and testing relatives, and the person's role in ongoing treatment such as regular drop use.
recommendations.context: Information is intended to support active participation in decisions.

recommendations.statement: Give practical advice about eye drop application, including punctal occlusion, devices and storage hygiene; required monitoring; assessment methods; likely appointment duration and help needed to attend, including avoiding driving soon after pupil dilatation; contacting the ECLO and the assistance available; support organisations and groups; compliance aids obtainable from a GP or community pharmacist; LVI, RVI, CVI and registration; and DVLA regulations.

document_sections.heading: Overview
document_sections.content: The guideline addresses diagnosis and management of glaucoma in adults aged 18 and over. It covers case-finding and referral for chronic open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension, as well as diagnosis, treatment and reassessment intended to prevent progression.

document_sections.heading: Who is it for?
document_sections.content: The intended readers are healthcare professionals; commissioners and providers of eye care; and adults who have chronic open angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension, or are at risk of glaucoma, together with their families and carers.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: People should participate in informed decisions about their care. The recommendations express NICE's judgement of the available evidence; clinicians should consider them alongside each person's circumstances, needs and preferences. They do not replace individual clinical judgement or consultation with the person and, where appropriate, their family, carers or guardian.

document_sections.heading: 1.1 Case-finding
document_sections.content: These recommendations concern primary eye care assessment before referral for diagnosis of chronic open angle glaucoma (COAG) and related conditions; case-finding is distinct from a sight test. Before referral, offer central visual field testing by standard automated perimetry, using a full-threshold or supra-threshold strategy; assess the optic nerve and fundus by stereoscopic slit lamp biomicroscopy, dilating the pupil if needed, and obtain optical coherence tomography (OCT) or an optic nerve head image if available; measure intraocular pressure (IOP) by Goldmann-type applanation tonometry; and assess peripheral anterior chamber configuration and depth by gonioscopy or, if unavailable or preferred by the person, by the van Herick test or OCT [2017]. Do not refer solely because of an IOP reading from non-contact tonometry [2017]. Do not re-refer someone discharged from hospital eye services following assessment for COAG or related conditions unless changed clinical circumstances require a new referral [2017]. Before referral, consider repeating visual field testing and IOP measurement on a different occasion to confirm a field defect or IOP of 24 mmHg or more, unless urgent or emergency referral is clinically indicated [2017]. After considering repeat measurements, refer if stereoscopic slit lamp biomicroscopy shows optic nerve head damage, a visual field defect is compatible with glaucoma, or Goldmann-type applanation tonometry shows IOP of 24 mmHg or more [2017]. Include every examination and test result with the referral [2017]. Advise those with IOP below 24 mmHg to keep attending their primary eye care professional regularly [2017]. Eye care services should include Goldmann-type applanation tonometry before referral for diagnosis, and service planners should consider referral filtering, such as repeat measures, enhanced case-finding or referral refinement [2017].

document_sections.heading: 1.2 Diagnosis
document_sections.content: For diagnosis of COAG and related conditions, offer standard automated perimetry with a central thresholding test, repeated if necessary to establish baseline severity; dilated stereoscopic slit lamp examination of the optic nerve and fundus; slit lamp mounted Goldmann applanation tonometry; gonioscopy to assess peripheral anterior chamber configuration and depth; and central corneal thickness (CCT) measurement [2017]. Follow professional or Department of Health and Social Care guidance to limit transmission of infectious agents during contact tonometry or gonioscopy, including applicable guidance on CJD and vCJD [2009]. If clinical circumstances prevent gonioscopy, such as an inability to participate because of physical or learning disabilities, use the van Herick assessment instead [2009]. Obtain an optic nerve head image at diagnosis as a baseline, for example a stereoscopic image or OCT [2009, amended 2017]. Consider an early post-referral appointment when the referral information raises clinical concern [2017]. At diagnosis of ocular hypertension (OHT), assess lifetime risk of future visual impairment in light of IOP, CCT, family history and life expectancy [2017].

document_sections.heading: 1.3 Standard practice for all assessments
document_sections.content: At every clinical encounter, make previous relevant COAG and OHT tests and images, relevant medical history, current systemic and topical medicines, the glaucoma medication history, and drug allergies and intolerances available to everyone involved in care [2009]. When standard examination methods are not feasible, use alternatives appropriate to the circumstances, including for people unable to participate because of physical or learning disabilities [2009]. Calibrate machines and measuring instruments regularly in accordance with their manufacturers' instructions [2009].

document_sections.heading: 1.4 Treatment
document_sections.content: Account for cognitive and physical impairment when choosing management and treatment [2017]. Before prescribing, check for relevant comorbidities and possible medicine interactions [2009].

document_sections.heading: Treatment for people with OHT
document_sections.content: Do not treat OHT when the person is not at risk of visual impairment during their lifetime. Instead, advise continued appointments with a primary eye care professional at clinically appropriate intervals [2017].

document_sections.heading: Initial treatment for people with OHT
document_sections.content: Offer 360° selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) to people with newly diagnosed OHT, IOP of 24 mmHg or more and lifetime risk of visual impairment, except when the condition is associated with pigment dispersion syndrome. Explain that 360° SLT may postpone eye drops and reduce, but not eliminate, the possibility of needing them; discuss the expected time until IOP improves, procedure-specific adverse effects and complications and their likely duration, and the possibility of another 360° SLT later [2022]. Consider another 360° SLT if an initially successful treatment subsequently loses effect [2022]. Offer a generic prostaglandin analogue (PGA) when OHT meets the same IOP and lifetime-risk criteria and the person declines 360° SLT, the procedure is unsuitable, interim treatment is needed while awaiting it, or additional IOP reduction is necessary after it. At first prescription, demonstrate eye drop instillation and observe the person performing it correctly [2022].

document_sections.heading: Ongoing treatment for people with OHT
document_sections.content: For IOP of 24 mmHg or more with intolerance of current treatment, offer another medicine: first an alternative generic PGA, then a beta-blocker if that is not tolerated. If neither is tolerated, offer a non-generic PGA, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, sympathomimetic, miotic or treatment combination [2017, amended 2022]. If treatment does not lower IOP enough to prevent progression to sight loss, offer a different therapeutic class—a beta-blocker, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor or sympathomimetic; concurrent topical medicines from different classes may be necessary [2009, amended 2017]. NICE technology appraisal guidance recommends latanoprost–netarsudil as an option to reduce IOP in adults with OHT (TA1009, 2024). If 360° SLT, medicines or both cannot lower IOP sufficiently to prevent progression to sight loss, refer to a consultant ophthalmologist to discuss other options [2009, amended 2022]. Offer preservative-free eye drops to a person with preservative allergy or clinically significant symptomatic ocular surface disease only when their risk of conversion to COAG is high [2009, amended 2017].

document_sections.heading: Treatment for people with suspected COAG
document_sections.content: Do not treat suspected COAG with IOP less than 24 mmHg unless lifetime risk of visual impairment warrants treatment. Advise continued visits to a primary eye care professional at clinically appropriate intervals [2017, amended 2022].

document_sections.heading: Stopping treatment for people with OHT or suspected COAG
document_sections.content: For a person with OHT or suspected COAG who has both low lifetime risk of visual impairment and acceptable IOP, discuss the advantages and disadvantages of stopping treatment. If the person chooses to stop, offer an IOP assessment in 1 month to 4 months and further reassessment when clinically indicated [2009].

document_sections.heading: Treatment for people with COAG
document_sections.content: In January 2022, use of mitomycin-C (MMC) in recommendations 1.4.14 and 1.4.22 to 1.4.24 was off label.

document_sections.heading: Treatment for people with advanced COAG
document_sections.content: Offer glaucoma surgery, with pharmacological augmentation using MMC when indicated, to people with advanced COAG, and explain the surgical benefits and risks [2009, amended 2022]. If someone presents with previously untreated advanced COAG and is awaiting glaucoma surgery, offer a generic PGA in the interim [2009, amended 2022]. If surgery is unsuitable or declined, use the options specified in recommendation 1.4.27.

document_sections.heading: Initial treatment for people with COAG
document_sections.content: Offer 360° SLT for newly diagnosed COAG that is not advanced, excluding cases associated with pigment dispersion syndrome. Explain that the procedure can delay eye drops and reduce, without eliminating, the likelihood of needing them; discuss how soon IOP might improve, the expected duration of procedure-specific adverse effects and complications, and the possibility of a later second 360° SLT [2022]. Consider a second 360° SLT if the benefit of a previously successful procedure declines [2022]. Offer a generic PGA if the person declines 360° SLT, it is unsuitable, an interim treatment is needed while waiting, or further IOP reduction is necessary after it to avert visual impairment. When eye drops are first prescribed, show the correct instillation technique and watch the person use it [2022].

document_sections.heading: Ongoing treatment for people with COAG
document_sections.content: Encourage continuation of the same medicine unless IOP reduction is insufficient to prevent sight-loss progression, optic nerve head damage or visual field defects progress, or the medicine cannot be tolerated [2009]. If a generic PGA has not reduced IOP enough, ask about adherence and check eye drop technique [2009, amended 2022]. When adherence and technique are satisfactory but IOP remains insufficiently controlled, offer 1 of these options: a beta-blocker, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor or sympathomimetic from another therapeutic class, with multiple topical classes if needed; 360° SLT; or glaucoma surgery augmented with MMC when indicated [2009, amended 2022]. If sight loss may progress despite medicines from 2 therapeutic classes, consider 360° SLT or MMC-augmented glaucoma surgery and explain surgical benefits and risks [2009, amended 2022]. For intolerance of a medicine, consider another class—a beta-blocker, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor or sympathomimetic—or preservative-free drops if preservative allergy or clinically significant symptomatic ocular surface disease is evident. Following treatment with medicines from 2 classes, consider 360° SLT or MMC-augmented glaucoma surgery [2009, amended 2022]. NICE technology appraisal guidance recommends latanoprost–netarsudil as an IOP-lowering option for adults with primary open-angle glaucoma (COAG) when a PGA alone has been inadequate, but only after a fixed-dose combination has also inadequately lowered IOP or when a fixed-dose combination containing beta-blockers is unsuitable (TA1009, 2024). If IOP remains insufficiently reduced after glaucoma surgery, offer 1 of pharmacological treatment, potentially combining topical classes; another glaucoma operation; 360° SLT; or cyclodiode laser treatment [2009, amended 2022]. For people with COAG, including advanced COAG, who decline surgery or cannot undergo it, offer 1 of pharmacological treatment, potentially combining topical classes; 360° SLT, for example with systemic comorbidities; or cyclodiode laser treatment [2009, amended 2022].

document_sections.heading: 1.5 Reassessment
document_sections.content: Follow-up testing and the timing of reassessment depend on clinical findings, IOP control and the risks of conversion, progression and sight loss.

document_sections.heading: Reassessment tests
document_sections.content: At every assessment of COAG, suspected COAG or OHT, offer slit lamp mounted Goldmann applanation tonometry and anterior segment slit lamp examination, adding van Herick peripheral anterior chamber depth assessment when clinically indicated [2017]. Repeat gonioscopy when indicated, including after an inconclusive examination or when anterior chamber angle status may have changed [2017]. When indicated, repeat standard automated central-threshold visual field testing in COAG or when a suspected field defect is under investigation for possible COAG [2009, amended 2017]. For OHT or suspected COAG with a previously normal field documented by standard automated central-threshold perimetry, use either a central-threshold or supra-threshold test when repeat testing is indicated [2009, amended 2017]. Once a field defect has been identified, maintain the same measurement strategy at subsequent visual field assessments [2009]. Reassess the optic nerve head when indicated, for example by stereoscopic slit lamp biomicroscopy or imaging [2017]. If stereoscopic examination identifies a change in optic nerve head status, obtain another image as a new baseline [2009]. If reassessment does not provide an adequate view of the nerve head and adjacent area, dilate the pupils before repeating stereoscopic examination or imaging [2009].

document_sections.heading: When to reassess
document_sections.content: At every assessment, reconsider the likelihood of conversion to COAG and of sight loss before setting the next appointment [2017]. Ask about general health and, when relevant, factors affecting adherence, including cognitive impairment and treatment adverse effects [2017]. Use clinical judgement within the recommended intervals, including when the effect of newly started treatment needs assessment.

document_sections.heading: People with treated OHT (baseline IOP 24 mmHg or more) and a normal optic nerve head and visual field at most recent assessment
document_sections.content: For treated OHT with baseline IOP of 24 mmHg or more and a normal optic nerve head and visual field at the latest assessment, judge IOP control and conversion risk clinically, then use table 1 to select the reassessment interval [2017].

document_sections.heading: Table 1 Time to next assessment for people being treated for OHT
document_sections.content: The table assigns the next assessment according to conversion status and IOP control. Its intervals cover reassessment between 1 month and 4 months, between 6 months and 12 months, or between 18 months and 24 months; detected conversion redirects care to COAG diagnosis and reassessment. Clinical judgement determines the appointment within an interval, including whether a new treatment needs review. Uncertain conversion can mean that sufficiently accurate information was unavailable because the person could not participate in assessment.

document_sections.heading: People with suspected COAG
document_sections.content: Use clinical judgement to determine IOP control and risk of conversion to COAG, considering optic nerve head damage and visual field defects; choose reassessment timing using table 2 [2017].

document_sections.heading: Table 2 Time to next assessment for people with suspected COAG
document_sections.content: The table relates conversion status and IOP control to the next assessment, with intervals of 1 month to 4 months, 6 months to 12 months, or 12 months to 18 months. Detected conversion leads to the COAG diagnosis and reassessment recommendations. Select an appointment within the interval using clinical judgement, including review of newly initiated treatment. Uncertain conversion may reflect insufficient reliable information when the person could not participate.

document_sections.heading: People with COAG
document_sections.content: Assess the risk that COAG will progress to sight loss using clinical judgement, and set follow-up according to table 3 [2017].

document_sections.heading: Table 3 Time to next assessment for people with COAG
document_sections.content: The table sets review intervals according to evidence of progression, clinical risk and IOP control: 1 month to 4 months, 1 month to 2 months, 12 months to 18 months, 6 months to 12 months, or 2 months to 6 months. Use clinical judgement within the applicable interval, including the need to evaluate recently started treatment. The accompanying text describes uncertain conversion as potentially resulting from insufficient accurate assessment information, such as inability to participate, although this table concerns progression.

document_sections.heading: Discharge back to primary care
document_sections.content: Return people to primary eye care if referral for OHT establishes that treatment is unnecessary or referral for suspected COAG establishes that COAG is no longer suspected. Advise regular primary eye care appointments at clinically appropriate intervals [2017]. Give the person a discharge summary, send a copy to their GP and, with consent, send relevant information to the primary eye care professional they nominate. Advise them to bring the summary to future sight tests [2017].

document_sections.heading: 1.6 Organisation of care
document_sections.content: Refer to a consultant ophthalmologist for consideration of a definitive diagnosis and management plan if optic nerve damage or a repeatable visual field defect is suspected, or if SLT is suitable [2009, amended 2022]. A suitably trained professional diagnosing OHT or suspected COAG and establishing a management plan should have a specialist qualification and relevant experience [2009, amended 2017]. An independent or non-medical prescribing qualification by itself, without a specialist qualification appropriate to glaucoma complexity, does not suffice for management [2017]. Professionals diagnosing OHT or suspected COAG, or making a preliminary identification of COAG, should be trained in detection and referral refinement, identify abnormalities on clinical assessment, understand diagnostic principles, and perform and interpret medical and ocular histories, differential diagnosis, slit lamp mounted Goldmann applanation tonometry, standard automated central-threshold and central supra-threshold perimetry, stereoscopic anterior segment slit lamp biomicroscopy, posterior segment examination by slit lamp binocular indirect ophthalmoscopy, gonioscopy, van Herick depth assessment and CCT measurement [2009]. Monitoring and treatment of OHT, suspected COAG or COAG should be provided by someone with specialist qualification, relevant experience and the ability to recognise a change in clinical status [2009, amended 2017]. Professionals making monitoring and treatment decisions should be trained to evaluate conversion risk, coexisting disease, sight-loss risk, clinical change, the pharmacology of IOP-lowering medicines, eligibility for 360° SLT, and treatment changes with their contraindications and interactions [2009, amended 2022]. Discuss whether and how to perform 360° SLT with the responsible consultant ophthalmologist; that consultant should support the professionals performing it. Training should cover suitability, laser safety, benefits and risks, discussions with patients and families or carers, and consent [2022]. With an established plan, a person with confirmed OHT or suspected COAG may be monitored, but not treated, by a suitably trained professional who knows these conditions, has relevant experience and can recognise clinical change. That professional should perform and interpret Goldmann applanation tonometry, central-threshold and central supra-threshold perimetry, stereoscopic anterior segment slit lamp examination, van Herick assessment and posterior segment examination by slit lamp binocular indirect ophthalmoscopy. Central supra-threshold perimetry may monitor OHT or suspected COAG when the field is normal [2009]. Professionals working independently of consultant ophthalmologist supervision bear full responsibility for the care they deliver [2009].

document_sections.heading: 1.7 Providing information
document_sections.content: Give people opportunities to discuss diagnosis, referral, prognosis, treatment and discharge so that they can participate actively in decisions, and provide accessible information at initial and later visits. Explain their particular condition—OHT, suspected COAG or COAG—its lifelong implications and likely preservation of sight; the absence of symptoms in OHT, suspected COAG and early COAG; that most people treated for COAG retain good quality of life without blindness; and that lost sight cannot be restored. Discuss treatment choices, how they work, adverse-effect frequency and severity, benefits and risks, possible familial occurrence and testing of relatives, and the person's role in regular eye drop use to preserve sight [2009, amended 2017]. Provide practical advice on eye drop technique, punctal occlusion, devices and storage hygiene; required monitoring; assessment methods; anticipated appointment length and assistance needed to attend, including the inadvisability of driving soon after pupil dilation; the eye clinic liaison officer (ECLO); support groups and organisations; aids such as dispensers from a GP or community pharmacist; Letter of Vision Impairment (LVI), Referral of Vision Impairment (RVI), Certificate of Vision Impairment (CVI) and registration; and Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) regulations [2009, amended 2017].

document_sections.heading: COAG and related conditions
document_sections.content: The related conditions covered here are chronic open angle glaucoma (COAG), also termed primary open-angle glaucoma, ocular hypertension (OHT), and suspected COAG.

document_sections.heading: Enhanced case-finding
document_sections.content: An enhanced community case-finding service uses slit lamp mounted Goldmann-type applanation tonometry, dilated slit lamp indirect biomicroscopy and further tests the healthcare professional considers necessary.

document_sections.heading: MMC
document_sections.content: Mitomycin-C is an antimetabolite administered early in trabeculectomy to limit excessive postoperative scarring and thereby lower the chance that the operation will fail.

document_sections.heading: Primary eye care professionals
document_sections.content: This group includes optometrists, GPs with a special interest in ophthalmology, and community orthoptists.

document_sections.heading: Referral filtering
document_sections.content: Referral filtering means checking accuracy before a hospital eye services referral. It can involve repeat measures, enhanced case-finding, referral refinement, hospital-based triage or administrative paper-based triage.

document_sections.heading: Referral refinement
document_sections.content: This is a 2-tier assessment: an enhanced examination validates an abnormality first found through case-finding or screening and goes beyond simple repeat measurement. The service tests for OHT and suspected COAG and interprets findings clinically. Independent specialist practitioners require the qualifications and experience specified for organising care; practitioners should be qualified to diagnose OHT and suspected glaucoma and perform gonioscopy to exclude angleclosure glaucoma.

document_sections.heading: Repeat measures
document_sections.content: This means measuring glaucoma-related diagnostic parameters again. A simple scheme may repeat only IOP; other schemes may also retest visual fields and other relevant ocular parameters when necessary.

document_sections.heading: Sight loss
document_sections.content: Glaucoma-related sight loss is visual damage producing blind areas in the field of vision. Early defects generally cause no symptoms, so affected people may be unaware; progression can lead to visual impairment and eventually symptoms.

document_sections.heading: Sight test
document_sections.content: A sight test establishes whether a visual defect exists and what might correct, remedy or relieve it. An optometrist must perform the examinations required by the Sight Testing (Examination and Prescription) (No 2) Regulations 1989, including internal and external eye examination and any further examination needed to identify signs of injury, disease or abnormality in the eye or elsewhere.

document_sections.heading: Visual impairment
document_sections.content: This is a marked reduction in vision that ordinary glasses or contact lenses cannot correct and that limits functioning in a visual environment.

document_sections.heading: 1 Risk tools to identify risk of developing chronic open angle glaucoma and risk of sight loss
document_sections.content: The committee proposes research into how well risk tools predict which people in the community are more likely to develop COAG and which people with COAG are more likely to lose sight.

document_sections.heading: 2 Long-term effectiveness of selective laser trabeculoplasty
document_sections.content: The proposed research compares the long-term clinical effectiveness and cost effectiveness of first-line selective laser trabeculoplasty against IOP-lowering eye drops in adults with OHT or COAG.

document_sections.heading: 3 An instrument to measure quality of life in people with glaucoma
document_sections.content: The committee calls for research to identify an appropriate measure of health-related quality of life for people with glaucoma.

document_sections.heading: 4 Optical coherence tomography for glaucoma
document_sections.content: The proposed research evaluates the effectiveness and cost effectiveness of optical coherence tomography in glaucoma diagnosis and monitoring.

document_sections.heading: 5 Referral filtering
document_sections.content: The committee proposes comparing the effectiveness and cost effectiveness of different pathways from case-finding to secondary ophthalmic assessment for detecting glaucoma, OHT and suspected glaucoma.

document_sections.heading: 6 Treatment for people with an intraocular pressure of 22 mmHg or 23 mmHg
document_sections.content: The proposed research examines the clinical effectiveness and cost effectiveness of treating IOP of 22 mmHg or 23 mmHg when optic discs and visual fields are normal.

document_sections.heading: Selective laser trabeculoplasty for people with ocular hypertension or chronic open angle glaucoma
document_sections.content: The rationale concerns recommendations 1.4.4, 1.4.5, 1.4.17 and 1.4.18 on initial and repeat 360° SLT for OHT or COAG.

document_sections.heading: Why the committee made the recommendations
document_sections.content: For the recommendations on 360° SLT, the committee regarded long-term visual field progression as the central outcome and IOP as a relevant surrogate because reducing it can lower the risk of optic nerve damage and sight loss. High-quality evidence showed no meaningful difference between 360° SLT and eye drops in achieving target IOP, health-related quality of life, overall adverse-event risk or adherence. Transient discomfort, blurred vision, photophobia and hyperaemia occurred with SLT. Rare complications are possible; corneal failure can follow SLT, although rare events were not identified in the evidence. At 12 months, first-line eye drops resulted in more people using drops and more people using more than 1 eye drop medicine than first-line 360° SLT. The cost-effectiveness evidence found first-line 360° SLT more effective and less costly than drops, with at least 90% probability that it was the more cost-effective option. Savings over time on drops outweighed the procedure's initial costs. The analysis associated 360° SLT with longer periods without drops or with fewer drops and slightly slower estimated glaucoma progression. The trial found no statistically significant direct quality-of-life benefit; additional natural-history data incorporated into the economic analysis suggested that quality of life was likely to improve. The analysis included costs and benefits of another 360° SLT when clinicians considered one necessary. Even assuming equal clinical effectiveness to drops, estimated lower overall costs made 360° SLT highly cost effective. The committee combined this evidence with clinical experience to recommend first-line 360° SLT for newly diagnosed OHT or non-advanced COAG. It excluded pigment dispersion syndrome because evidence for 360° SLT in that group was absent and the committee considered drops more suitable. Approximately 15% of people in the SLT arm of the cost-effectiveness analyses received another procedure within the first year. The committee considered another 360° SLT appropriate when the effect of a successful first procedure wanes and IOP rises, with a clinician judging the risk of COAG progression or OHT conversion. The responsible consultant ophthalmologist should decide whether to repeat it, consistent with the LiGHT trial procedure. The committee generally considered at least 6 months of IOP reduction necessary to judge treatment successful, while allowing clinician discretion. It identified a lack of long-term evidence on visual field and optic nerve head progression and noted that patients place greater importance on vision than surrogate outcomes such as IOP. It therefore proposed research on long-term 360° SLT effectiveness with follow-up of 3 years or more, 5 years and 10 years.

document_sections.heading: Impact on other recommendations
document_sections.content: When recommending 360° SLT, the committee reviewed its implications for other guidance and amended recommendations as needed, considering their original evidence and its clinical experience.

document_sections.heading: How the recommendations might affect practice
document_sections.content: For first-line 360° SLT, the committee anticipated a substantial practice change as more newly diagnosed people with OHT or COAG become eligible. Larger centres might receive more referrals and need more clinics each week. Overall costs were not expected to rise substantially because first-line 360° SLT, including equipment purchase and maintenance, cost less than first-line drops in the evidence. Spending would shift away from prescriptions and toward SLT equipment and staffing.

document_sections.heading: Generic PGAs for people with OHT or COAG
document_sections.content: This rationale concerns recommendations 1.4.6 and 1.4.19 on generic PGA eye drops for OHT or COAG.

document_sections.heading: Why the committee made the recommendations
document_sections.content: For generic PGAs, the committee revised the 2017 approach in light of the 2022 first-line 360° SLT recommendations. It retained generic PGA drops when a person prefers not to have 360° SLT or the procedure is unsuitable, noting that PGA drops had been first-line treatment in the 2017 guideline and the LiGHT trial. It also specified that, when drops are first prescribed, professionals should demonstrate instillation and observe the person to confirm correct technique.

document_sections.heading: Organisation of care
document_sections.content: This rationale addresses recommendations 1.6.6 and 1.6.7 on professional training, consultant involvement and provision of 360° SLT.

document_sections.heading: Why the committee made the recommendations
document_sections.content: For organisation of care, the committee anticipated that first-line 360° SLT could require a different service structure and multidisciplinary team. A person for whom the procedure is suitable should be referred to a consultant ophthalmologist. Professionals should agree the decision and approach with the responsible consultant, whose support can enable specialty doctors, associate specialists, specialist nurses, optometrists and allied health professionals to perform 360° SLT. Training should address suitability, safety, benefits, risks, discussions with patients and families or carers, and consent. In the LiGHT trial, treating surgeons received training before recruitment, and its chief investigator, a consultant ophthalmic surgeon, observed each surgeon perform at least 1 laser treatment.

document_sections.heading: How the recommendations might affect practice
document_sections.content: For organisation of care, the committee expected a substantial practice change because professionals carrying out 360° SLT will need training and support.

document_sections.heading: Context
document_sections.content: The guideline's scope expanded in 2017 to include referral, filtering models, case-finding tests and referral thresholds for COAG, suspected COAG and OHT. That update also revised diagnosis and reassessment tests, IOP-lowering pharmacological treatment intended to preserve visual fields, and prognosis-dependent review intervals. A reassessment of OHT treatment indications removed the need to know corneal thickness when deciding whether to treat and established a single 24 mmHg threshold for referral and treatment. Changes in medicine costs, recognised short- and long-term IOP variability, and the uneven relation between higher pressure and risk supported simpler treatment criteria. IOP control remains central; disease severity, visual field change, optic disc morphology and likelihood of progressive sight loss guide treatment intensity and continuing care. Review at every visit supports flexible decisions about follow-up and treatment, including stopping therapy when lifetime visual-impairment risk is low. New evidence since 2017 prompted updated recommendations on first-line 360° SLT for OHT and COAG. Sections on visual field test accuracy, surgery, and information, education and support for adherence were not updated because no new evidence was found.

document_sections.heading: Update information
document_sections.content: The January 2022 evidence review led to new OHT and COAG treatment and care-organisation recommendations, identified by [2022]. Other wording changes clarified references to glaucoma surgery and the role of 360° SLT, including treatment for suspected COAG when lifetime visual-impairment risk is present; these carry [2009, amended 2022] or [2017, amended 2022]. Recommendations marked [2009] last underwent evidence review in 2009. The November 2017 update replaced CG85 and added case-finding, diagnosis, reassessment and treatment recommendations marked [2017]; changes without a new evidence review carry [2009, amended 2017].
